segs.text: Module four, objective two. Glomerular filtration, tubular secretion and tubular reabsorption, the three processes by which the kidney handles a drug. In the nephron, drug passes from the blood across the glomerulus into the tubule, and the tubular lumen is the fluid space inside that tubule. The amount of drug that ends up in the urine is the net result of three processes: filtration and secretion add drug to the lumen, and reabsorption moves drug from the lumen back into the blood.

card.m: filtration, secretion → add drug to the lumen
reabsorption → lumen back to the blood

segs.text: Glomerular filtration is passive diffusion across the glomerulus, so it needs no energy. The glomerular filtration rate, G F R, is the volume of fluid the glomeruli filter from the blood per unit time, and in normal kidneys it averages one hundred twenty milliliters per minute. Only drug that is not bound to plasma protein is filtered, so the textbook notes that a heavily bound drug is filtered less and has a longer half-life. Active tubular secretion uses a transporter and energy to move drug from the blood into the urine, so it removes drug on top of filtration. Tubular reabsorption moves some drug from the urine in the tubule back into the blood, so it takes away from what was removed.

card.m: GFR: average 120 mL/min, a volume per time
only unbound drug is filtered: more binding → less filtered

segs.text: Renal clearance, Cl R, the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time by the kidney, is a volume per time like G F R, so the two can be compared. A drug that is only filtered is cleared at about the filtration rate, one hundred twenty milliliters per minute. If a transporter also secretes it, more plasma is cleared of drug than filtration alone can clear, so renal clearance rises above one hundred twenty. If some filtered drug returns to the blood, less is cleared, so renal clearance falls below one hundred twenty. Cl R equals filtration plus secretion minus reabsorption, in milliliters per minute, so the two added terms raise it and the subtracted term lowers it.

card.m: Cl<sub>R</sub> and GFR: both volumes per time, mL/min
a reasoning rule, not on the equation sheet

segs.text: Stated as a rule, reabsorption occurs if the renal clearance is less than the clearance by filtration. She allows a margin around the filtration value of one hundred twenty milliliters per minute. She said, I'm saying one hundred twenty. If it's one hundred nineteen, one hundred twenty one let's call that filtration. If it's two hundred fifty, then let's assume that we've got some active secretion going on. A renal clearance given in liters per hour has to be put in the same units before the comparison: one hundred twenty milliliters per minute is seven point two liters per hour.

In her Module six practice set, a drug has a total body clearance of fifty two point nine five and a renal clearance of thirty four point seven two, both in milliliters per minute per seventy kilograms, and the probable mechanism of renal clearance is asked. The mechanism is read from renal clearance alone, so the total is set aside, and the renal clearance is already in milliliters per minute. A renal clearance of thirty four point seven two milliliters per minute is well below the filtration rate of one hundred twenty milliliters per minute, so the kidney clears less plasma of this drug than filtration alone would. Some filtered drug must be returning to the blood, and the mechanism is glomerular filtration with tubular reabsorption.

card.m: use Cl<sub>R</sub> only; mL/min, no conversion

segs.text: Her review poll gave a renal clearance of forty five milliliters per minute for an antibiotic and asked what can be inferred. The key is that the drug is filtered and reabsorbed, because forty five is below the filtration rate. The option some evidence of renal impairment is the trap: a drug's renal clearance, read against the average one hundred twenty milliliters per minute, describes how the kidney handles that drug, while the patient's kidney function is judged from creatinine clearance, in objective three. For the same reason, a value below one hundred twenty does not mean reduced filtration. A second trap compares a renal clearance in liters per hour with one hundred twenty milliliters per minute without converting. Objective four explains what controls how much filtered drug is reabsorbed.

card.m: ✗ renal impairment: Cl<sub>R</sub> vs 120 mL/min describes the drug; the patient's kidneys → CrCl (objective 3)
objective 4: urine pH and pK<sub>a</sub> → reabsorption
